body:
Why energy is important to Gujarat

Gujarat's economy depends on energy for manufacturing, agriculture, transport, commercial activity and household needs. Petroleum fuels vehicles and provides raw materials for petrochemical industries. Natural gas supplies industrial heat, supports fertiliser production and reaches homes and vehicles through distribution networks. Electricity operates factories, irrigation pumps, railways, businesses and domestic appliances.

The state's energy economy has 3 important geographical advantages: a long coastline with major ports, established industrial centres and regions suitable for solar and wind power. These features connect Gujarat with both domestic energy resources and international fuel markets.

Energy economy refers to the production, import, processing, transportation, distribution and use of energy resources, together with the industries and infrastructure involved in these activities.

Energy resources and energy carriers

An energy resource contains or provides energy that can be used. Coal, crude oil, natural gas, sunlight, wind and flowing water are examples. An energy carrier delivers energy in a usable form. Electricity and refined petroleum products are important carriers because energy from primary resources has already been converted or processed into a form suitable for consumers.

Electricity is particularly useful because it can be generated from several different sources. A factory may receive electricity generated from coal, solar panels, wind turbines, hydropower or nuclear energy through the same interconnected electricity system. The factory does not need a separate electrical connection for each source.

Primary and secondary energy

  • Primary energy: Energy available from natural resources before conversion, such as coal, crude petroleum, natural gas, sunlight and flowing water.
  • Secondary energy: Energy obtained after converting primary energy, such as electricity produced in a power station or petrol obtained by refining crude oil.

A refinery processes crude petroleum into several useful products, while a power station converts an energy source into electricity. These are different activities even when both use fossil fuels.

How energy reaches consumers

Gujarat has 2 major networks that should not be confused. The petroleum and gas system moves physical fuels through ports, terminals, refineries, storage facilities, pipelines and other transport arrangements. The electricity system generates electrical energy and carries it through transmission and distribution networks.

Imported crude oil may be unloaded at a coastal terminal and transported to a refinery. The refinery produces fuels and petrochemical feedstocks that are subsequently transported to markets. Imported liquefied natural gas follows another route: it is received at an LNG terminal, converted back into gas and carried through pipelines. Electricity follows a third route, from generating stations through the grid to consumers.

These pathways may overlap in their final uses. An industrial plant can purchase electricity for machinery, natural gas for heating and petroleum-derived materials for manufacturing. Consequently, electricity demand and total energy demand are not identical.

Renewable and non-renewable resources

Non-renewable resources, including coal, petroleum and natural gas, are consumed much faster than geological processes can replace them. Renewable resources, such as sunlight, wind and naturally replenished water flows, can provide energy repeatedly, although their availability varies with weather and location.

Another useful classification is fossil versus non-fossil energy. Solar, wind, hydro and nuclear electricity are non-fossil sources. However, nuclear energy is not normally classified as renewable because it uses finite mineral fuel. The terms renewable, non-fossil and pollution-free therefore do not mean exactly the same thing.

Prelims focus

  • Coal, petroleum and natural gas are fossil fuels.
  • Electricity is a secondary form of energy that can be produced from different primary sources.
  • Gujarat's ports connect imported crude oil and LNG with inland energy markets.
  • Petroleum refining, gas transmission and electricity transmission perform different functions.
  • Trap: Nuclear energy is non-fossil but is not classified as renewable energy.

[References: NCERT, Class 8 Geography, Resources and Development, Chapter 3, 'Mineral and Power Resources,' printed pp. 30–36; NCERT, Class 11 Economics, Indian Economic Development, Chapter 8, 'Infrastructure,' section 8.5, printed pp. 144–149; NCERT, Class 12 Geography, India: People and Economy, Chapter 7, 'Mineral and Energy Resources,' printed pp. 76–83.]

title: The Structure of Gujarat's Energy Economy

body:
Petroleum resources in Gujarat

Crude petroleum is a naturally occurring mixture of hydrocarbons found in suitable geological formations. It is generally associated with sedimentary basins, where organic matter was transformed over geological time under appropriate conditions of burial, temperature and pressure.

The Cambay Basin, also called the Khambhat Basin, is an important petroleum-bearing region of Gujarat. Established oil-producing locations include Ankleshwar, Kalol and Mehsana. Other Gujarat oilfield names recorded in Indian geographical literature include Nawagam, Kosamba and Lunej.

Extracting petroleum from an oilfield is an upstream activity. Transporting, processing and marketing it involve subsequent stages of the petroleum industry. Oil extracted within Gujarat is only one possible source of refinery feedstock. Gujarat also processes imported crude oil received through maritime facilities.

Why crude oil must be refined

Crude petroleum is not a single finished fuel. It contains different hydrocarbon compounds with different properties and boiling ranges. A petroleum refinery separates and processes these compounds to produce useful materials.

Basic stages of refining

  1. Crude oil receipt: Oil reaches the refinery through pipelines or other suitable transport arrangements.
  2. Separation: Fractional distillation separates groups of hydrocarbons mainly according to differences in their boiling ranges.
  3. Further processing: Some fractions undergo additional treatment or conversion to obtain products with the required properties.
  4. Product movement: Finished fuels and intermediate materials are supplied to consumers or other industries.

Important refinery products include petrol, diesel, aviation turbine fuel, liquefied petroleum gas, kerosene and lubricating materials. Refineries also produce streams such as naphtha that can be used as feedstocks in petrochemical manufacturing. The exact product range varies among refineries.

Refining is not the same as petrochemical manufacturing. A refinery processes crude oil and produces fuels and intermediate streams. A petrochemical plant uses suitable hydrocarbon feedstocks to manufacture materials for chemicals, plastics, synthetic fibres and other products.

Major refineries and their locations

Gujarat contains important refining facilities operated by IndianOil, Reliance Industries and Nayara Energy. Their locations illustrate the importance of industrial markets, ports and transport connections.

The following are installed refining capacities as on 1 April 2026, published by the Government of India's Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell. Capacity is expressed in million metric tonnes per annum (MMTPA).

RefineryLocationOperatorCapacity (MMTPA)
KoyaliNear VadodaraIndianOil13.70
Jamnagar refineryJamnagarReliance Industries33.00
Jamnagar SEZ refineryJamnagarReliance Industries35.20
Vadinar refineryVadinarNayara Energy20.00

The 2 Reliance refinery entries together represent 68.20 MMTPA at Jamnagar. Adding the 4 entries gives Gujarat a combined listed refining capacity of 101.90 MMTPA on the stated date. This is a measure of annual processing capability, not the quantity of crude oil extracted from Gujarat's oilfields and not the actual quantity processed during a particular year.

Why the locations matter

Jamnagar and Vadinar benefit from access to the western coastline, where large quantities of crude oil can be received by sea. Their petroleum products can serve domestic and international markets. Koyali, located inland near Vadodara, demonstrates that a refinery need not be beside a producing oilfield or on the seashore. Pipeline connections and nearby demand centres are also important location factors.

Petroleum refining is connected with Gujarat's chemical and manufacturing economy. Refined fuels support transport and industry, while hydrocarbon feedstocks support other manufacturing processes. The presence of a refinery can therefore encourage related activities, but every chemical factory is not itself a refinery.

Prelims focus

  • The Cambay or Khambhat Basin is an important petroleum-bearing basin of Gujarat.
  • Ankleshwar, Kalol and Mehsana are associated with petroleum resources.
  • Koyali refinery is near Vadodara; Jamnagar and Vadinar are major coastal refining locations.
  • PPAC recorded 101.90 MMTPA of refining capacity across the 4 Gujarat refinery entries on 1 April 2026.
  • MMTPA means million metric tonnes per annum.
  • Trap: Refining capacity does not indicate crude-oil production or actual annual refinery throughput.

[References: NCERT, Class 8 Science, Chapter 5, 'Coal and Petroleum,' printed pp. 58–62; NCERT, Class 12 Geography, India: People and Economy, Chapter 7, 'Mineral and Energy Resources,' printed pp. 80–82, and Chapter 8, 'Manufacturing Industries,' section on industrial location; Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell, Government of India, 'Installed Refining Capacity,' company-wise table dated 1 April 2026, consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Petroleum Resources, Refineries and Ports in Gujarat

body:
Natural gas as a source of energy and industrial raw material

Natural gas is a fossil fuel consisting mainly of methane. It may occur along with petroleum or in separate gas deposits. It is used for cooking, industrial heating, power generation and the manufacture of products such as ammonia used in fertiliser production.

Natural gas can be transported through pipelines in its gaseous form. When a large quantity must cross the sea without a connecting pipeline, it is often transported as liquefied natural gas (LNG).

What happens at an LNG terminal?

Natural gas is cooled to approximately -162°C at near-atmospheric pressure to convert it into LNG. In liquid form, its volume is approximately 1/600 of the volume it occupies as a gas under comparable reference conditions. This reduction makes shipment in insulated LNG carriers practical.

At an import terminal, LNG is unloaded and stored in insulated tanks. It is subsequently warmed in a process called regasification, which converts the liquid back into natural gas. The gas can then enter transmission pipelines after the required processing and handling.

Major LNG terminals in Gujarat

The Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board's Annual Statistical Report 2025–26 identifies the following Gujarat LNG import and regasification terminals within India's operational terminal network for that reporting period.

TerminalGujarat locationMain significance
DahejBharuch districtMajor LNG import and regasification centre
HaziraSurat regionLNG import and regasification serving gas markets
MundraKachchh districtCoastal LNG import and regasification facility
ChharaGir Somnath districtLNG terminal commissioned in 2025

Terminal capacities and utilisation change with expansions, commissioning and operating conditions. A terminal's regasification capacity is its rated ability to process LNG; its utilisation measures how much of that capacity is actually used. A proposed terminal should never be counted as operational merely because its project has been announced.

The difference between gas transmission and city gas distribution

Once natural gas enters a pipeline system, different networks serve different purposes:

  • Natural gas transmission network: Carries large quantities of gas between supply points, industrial areas and regional delivery points.
  • City Gas Distribution (CGD): Delivers gas within authorised geographical areas to households, commercial establishments, industries and vehicle-fuelling facilities.
  • Direct industrial supply: Some large users are connected through arrangements suitable for their substantial gas requirements.

Gujarat developed an extensive pipeline network historically associated with Gujarat State Petronet Limited (GSPL). Following a corporate restructuring effective 1 May 2026, the gas transmission business became part of GSPL Transmission Limited (GTL). GTL reported approximately 2,878 km of medium-to-high-pressure gas transmission pipelines as on 31 March 2026.

The former Gujarat Gas Limited was renamed Gujarat Energy Limited with effect from 14 May 2026. These corporate changes should not be confused with a change in the physical meaning of transmission and city gas distribution. The Petroleum and Natural Gas Regulatory Board (PNGRB) regulates relevant natural gas pipeline and city gas distribution activities under its statutory framework.

LNG, CNG, PNG and LPG are not interchangeable terms

TermMeaningCommon use or feature
LNGLiquefied natural gasNatural gas cooled to liquid form, especially for shipping and storage
CNGCompressed natural gasNatural gas stored under pressure; commonly used as vehicle fuel
PNGPiped natural gasNatural gas supplied through pipelines to consumers
LPGLiquefied petroleum gasMainly propane and butane; commonly supplied in cylinders

Although LNG, CNG and PNG involve natural gas, their names describe different forms of storage or delivery. LPG is a different fuel mixture. LNG is usually regasified before being supplied through the conventional gas transmission network.

Why the gas grid matters to Gujarat

Industries are not always located at the point where gas enters the country. The gas grid links coastal import terminals and other gas supply sources with inland industrial and urban markets. It can support chemical plants, fertiliser production, ceramic manufacturing and gas-based power generation.

The network improves access to gas, but it does not eliminate supply risk. Imported LNG remains exposed to international prices, shipping conditions and external supply disruptions. Adequate terminal capacity is useful only when gas is available and the onward pipeline network can deliver it.

Prelims focus

  • LNG is natural gas cooled to approximately -162°C.
  • Regasification converts imported LNG back into gaseous natural gas.
  • Dahej, Hazira, Mundra and Chhara were listed as operational Gujarat LNG terminals in the 2025–26 reporting period.
  • GTL became the operator of the former GSPL gas transmission business through restructuring effective 1 May 2026.
  • PNG is supplied through pipelines; CNG is compressed natural gas commonly used in vehicles.
  • Trap: LPG is not another name for LNG.

[References: NCERT, Class 8 Science, Chapter 5, 'Coal and Petroleum,' printed pp. 60–62; Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited, 'Liquefied Natural Gas,' sections 'LNG' and 'LNG Terminals,' consulted 16 November 2026; PNGRB, Annual Statistical Report 2025–26, Chapter 4, LNG terminal tables, published 30 September 2026; GSPL Transmission Limited, 'Genesis,' pipeline and restructuring details, consulted 16 November 2026; Gujarat Energy Limited, corporate name-change disclosure dated 16 May 2026.]
